lead: Unit 7 covers the analog blocks that shape, generate and convert signals: active filters, waveform generators, multivibrators, the 555 timer, the PLL, and DACs and ADCs. After this unit you can design a second-order filter from a specification, set the frequency of a square or triangle generator, wire a 555 as an astable or monostable, and compute the output of an R-2R DAC and the code from a dual-slope ADC.
about: The unit moves from shaping a signal to generating it to converting it. Chapter 7.1 gives the four filter responses and the one-op-amp RC circuit behind each. Chapter 7.2 adds the second-order tools that real filter specifications demand: Butterworth and Chebyshev approximations and the Sallen-Key section. Chapter 7.3 shows multi-op-amp structures that give every response at once, and the switched-capacitor idea that makes filters tunable on an IC. Chapters 7.4 to 7.6 use the same positive-feedback loop to build square, triangle and sawtooth waves, then multivibrators, then the 555 timer. Chapter 7.7 closes a loop around a voltage-controlled oscillator to make a phase-locked loop. Chapters 7.8 and 7.9 handle conversion: resistor-ladder DACs first, then the four standard ADC architectures.

chapters.idea: One op-amp with resistors and capacitors gives four standard frequency responses, and each is read off a Bode plot by its cut-off frequency and its roll-off.
chapters.depth: First-order active sections for low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop, each built from one op-amp, two resistors and one or two capacitors. Cut-off f_c = 1/(2πRC), where R is in ohms and C in farads; pass-band gain set by the feedback resistors; roll-off of 20 dB per decade (about 6 dB per octave) per pole; the −3 dB point. Band-pass as a low-pass cascaded with a high-pass, band-stop as a summed low-pass plus high-pass or as a twin-T notch. Ideal versus practical response, since some syllabi open the topic this way. Hand sketching of the magnitude plot. Depth: read f_c and gain from a schematic, and compute the output amplitude at a given frequency.

figure.aria: Four curves against normalised frequency f/f_c: the low-pass falls, the high-pass rises, the band-pass peaks at 1 and the band-stop drops to zero at 1.

chapters.example: Design a first-order active low-pass filter with a cut-off of 1 kHz and a pass-band gain of magnitude 2. Take C = 10 nF. Find R and the gain at 10 kHz. R = 1/(2π × 1000 × 10 × 10⁻⁹) = 15.9 kΩ. A gain of 2 is 6 dB. At 10 kHz the frequency is one decade above f_c, so the response drops by 20 dB: 6 − 20 = −14 dB.
chapters.trap: Putting R in kΩ and C in µF straight into 1/(2πRC) without converting to ohms and farads, and writing the roll-off as 20 dB per octave instead of 20 dB per decade.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6: inverting amplifier, virtual ground, input impedance. Unit 3: cut-off frequency and Bode magnitude plots.
chapters.leave: Second-order design, Q and filter approximations to Chapter 7.2. Sine-wave oscillators to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Real filter specifications are met by choosing an approximation order, splitting it into second-order sections with a known Q, and building each section with a Sallen-Key circuit.
chapters.depth: Butterworth (maximally flat) and Chebyshev (equal-ripple) approximations; order n, ripple in dB, damping factor and pole Q. Butterworth second-order Q = 0.707; a fourth-order Butterworth splits into Q = 0.541 and Q = 1.307. Frequency and impedance scaling, and the low-pass to high-pass and low-pass to band-pass transformations. Sallen-Key equal-component low-pass and high-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), Q = 1/(3 − K), K = 1 + R_f/R_1, valid for K < 3. The single-op-amp positive-feedback band-pass that some syllabi call the Deliyannis-Friend circuit. Depth: from a specification choose the order, split into sections, pick C, compute R and the gain resistors.

figure.aria: A top-to-bottom design flow from filter specifications through order, section Q values and component values to a final Bode plot check.

chapters.example: Design a second-order Butterworth low-pass with f_c = 2 kHz using the equal-component Sallen-Key circuit. Take C = 10 nF. R = 1/(2π × 2000 × 10 × 10⁻⁹) = 7.96 kΩ, so use 8.2 kΩ 1% parts. The Butterworth second-order Q is 0.707, so K = 3 − 1/0.707 = 3 − 1.414 = 1.586. With R_1 = 10 kΩ, R_f = 0.586 × 10 kΩ = 5.86 kΩ, so use 5.9 kΩ.
chapters.trap: Taking Q = 1 for a Butterworth section, and forgetting that the Sallen-Key gain must stay below 3 or the positive feedback turns the filter into an oscillator.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1. Unit 3: Bode plots and roll-off. Unit 4: gain and phase margins and the idea of a stability limit.
chapters.leave: Multi-op-amp biquads and switched-capacitor filters to Chapter 7.3. Detailed approximation tables to later courses.

chapters.idea: Two integrators plus a summer in a loop produce low-pass, band-pass and high-pass outputs at the same time, and on an IC a switched capacitor can replace the resistor so the response is set by a clock ratio.
chapters.depth: State-variable (Kerwin-Huelsman-Newcomb) filter: summer gives high-pass, first integrator gives band-pass, second integrator gives low-pass; summing the three outputs gives a notch, so the block is called a universal filter. Centre frequency and Q set independently by resistor ratios. Tow-Thomas biquad, another multi-op-amp form some syllabi list. Switched-capacitor filters, which only a few universities teach: a capacitor C switched at f_clk behaves as R_eq = 1/(f_clk C), so cut-off is a ratio of capacitor values times f_clk, giving an accurate, tunable, IC-friendly filter. Sinusoidal oscillator built from a narrow band-pass section, also in some syllabi. Depth: identify each output, compute f_0 and Q, size the clock for a target cut-off.

figure.aria: A summer feeding two integrators in a closed loop, with the high-pass, band-pass and low-pass outputs taken at successive nodes.

chapters.example: A switched-capacitor resistor uses C = 1 pF switched at f_clk = 100 kHz. R_eq = 1/(f_clk C) = 1/(100 × 10³ × 1 × 10⁻¹²) = 10 MΩ. Use it as the input resistor of an integrator with a 1 pF feedback capacitor. The integrator's unity-gain frequency is 1/(2π R_eq C) = 1/(2π × 10⁷ × 10⁻¹²) = 15.9 kHz, which is f_clk/(2π).
chapters.trap: Believing a switched-capacitor filter can process signals near f_clk. The clock sets the sampling rate, so the input must stay below f_clk/2 or the output aliases.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.2. Unit 6: op-amp integrator, virtual ground, summer.
chapters.leave: Clock feedthrough, charge injection and anti-aliasing details to later courses. Sine oscillators to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A comparator with hysteresis and an integrator connected in a loop generate a square wave and a triangular wave, and an unequal charge and discharge makes a sawtooth.
chapters.depth: Square wave from a Schmitt trigger: output saturates at ±V_sat and the thresholds sit at ±βV_sat with β = R_1/(R_1 + R_2). Triangle wave by integrating that square wave with an RC integrator. Frequency f = 1/(4βRC) and triangle amplitude ±βV_sat. Sawtooth by steering the charge and discharge through different resistors with a diode, or by setting a duty cycle away from 50%. RC relaxation oscillator with a single op-amp, and the same idea inside a 555. Duty-cycle control with a potentiometer. Depth: compute frequency and amplitude, sketch both waveforms in correct phase, and explain how to change duty cycle without changing frequency much.

figure.aria: A Schmitt trigger and an integrator connected in a loop, with the square wave tapped at the trigger and the triangle at the integrator.

chapters.example: A Schmitt trigger with output ±12 V has R_1 = 10 kΩ to ground and R_2 = 20 kΩ to the output, so β = 10/(10 + 20) = 1/3 and the thresholds are ±4 V. The integrator uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. f = 1/(4βRC) = 1/(4 × 0.333 × 10 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹) = 1/(1.333 × 10⁻⁴) = 7.5 kHz. The triangle amplitude is ±βV_sat = ±4 V.
chapters.trap: Mixing up which op-amp gives which output, and leaving β out of the frequency formula so the answer depends only on RC.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6: comparator, Schmitt trigger, integrator. Chapter 7.3: the integrator loop.
chapters.leave: Sine-wave oscillators to Unit 4. Precision function-generator ICs to later courses.

chapters.idea: Two cross-coupled transistors or gates have two stable states, and the way the circuit leaves and re-enters those states gives the astable, monostable and bistable behaviours.
chapters.depth: Astable (free-running), monostable (one-shot) and bistable (latch, flip-flop) built from two cross-coupled BJTs or from logic gates, with the collector-coupled versions worked in full. Astable period T = 0.69(R_B1C1 + R_B2C2), with each capacitor charging through its base resistor and the state changing when the capacitor reaches about 0 V. Monostable pulse width T = 0.69RC, triggered by an edge shorter than the pulse. Bistable with SET and RESET inputs, and its use as a Schmitt trigger or a memory cell. Emitter-coupled monostable, which some syllabi include. Depth: narrate the charging path that ends each state and compute period or pulse width.

figure.aria: Three timing lanes: a free-running square that keeps toggling, a single triggered pulse that returns low, and a level that stays high after a set.

chapters.example: A collector-coupled astable uses C1 = C2 = 10 nF and R_B1 = R_B2 = 47 kΩ. T = 0.69(R_B1C1 + R_B2C2) = 1.38 × 47 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.65 ms, so f = 1/T = 1.54 kHz. Make one base resistor switchable to a trigger input and the same circuit becomes a monostable with pulse width 0.69 × 47 kΩ × 10 nF = 0.32 ms.
chapters.trap: Using 0.69RC as the full astable period instead of one half period, and forgetting that the monostable needs a trigger pulse shorter than the output pulse.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: BJT as a switch and the charging of a capacitor through a resistor. Unit 4: positive feedback and the Barkhausen condition.
chapters.leave: Emitter-coupled Schmitt trigger design to Unit 6. Timer IC versions to Chapter 7.6.

chapters.idea: The 555 packs two comparators, a latch and a discharge transistor around a three-resistor divider, so two external resistors and one capacitor set any astable or monostable timing.
chapters.depth: Internal block diagram: three equal 5 kΩ resistors set 2/3 V_CC and 1/3 V_CC, the upper and lower comparators drive an RS latch, the latch drives the discharge transistor and the output stage. Pin functions and the reset and control-voltage pins. Astable: T_H = 0.693(R_A + R_B)C, T_L = 0.693 R_B C, f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C), duty cycle = (R_A + R_B)/(R_A + 2R_B), always above 50% in the plain circuit; a diode across R_B fixes it. Monostable: T = 1.1RC. Applications: LED flasher, tone generator, missing-pulse detector, PWM with a modulating voltage on pin 5. Depth: choose R_A, R_B and C for a target frequency and duty cycle, and explain why the capacitor charges and discharges through different paths.

figure.aria: The 555 internals from Vcc through the three-resistor divider to the two comparators, the flip-flop, the discharge transistor and the output stage.

chapters.example: An astable 555 has R_A = 10 kΩ, R_B = 47 kΩ and C = 10 nF. T_H = 0.693 × 57 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.395 ms and T_L = 0.693 × 47 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.326 ms. T = 0.721 ms, so f = 1.39 kHz, and the duty cycle is 0.395/0.721 = 54.8%. The same parts wired as a monostable give a pulse of 1.1 × 47 kΩ × 10 nF = 0.52 ms.
chapters.trap: Treating both halves of the astable period as equal, and using 0.693RC instead of 1.1RC for the monostable pulse width.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.5 for the multivibrator idea. Unit 6: comparator, hysteresis, Schmitt trigger.
chapters.leave: 555 as a VCO to Chapter 7.7. Power-driver and PWM motor applications to later courses.

chapters.idea: A phase-locked loop compares the phase of a voltage-controlled oscillator with an input and drives the oscillator until the two match, so the output frequency follows the input.
chapters.depth: Blocks: phase detector (XOR gate or analog multiplier), loop filter (low-pass), VCO, feedback path. VCO characteristic f_out = f_0 + K_vco V_c, where f_0 is the free-running frequency and K_vco is in Hz per volt. Lock condition: zero phase error after the loop settles. Capture range (the band in which the loop can acquire lock) and lock range (the wider band in which it holds lock once locked); lock time and static phase error. The 565 and the 4046, which some syllabi use, with the 565 free-running frequency f_0 = 1.2/(4R_1C_1). Uses: FM demodulation, frequency multiplication with a divider in the feedback path, clock recovery. Depth: given f_0 and K_vco, compute the output frequency for a control voltage and state whether the loop locks.

figure.aria: A phase detector, loop filter and VCO in a closed loop, with the VCO output fed back to the detector and the control voltage between filter and VCO.

chapters.example: A 565 PLL has R_1 = 12 kΩ and C_1 = 2.5 nF. Its free-running frequency is f_0 = 1.2/(4R_1C_1) = 1.2/(4 × 12 × 10³ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁹) = 10 kHz. The VCO gain is 6 kHz/V. A control voltage of +0.5 V moves the output to 10 + 3 = 13 kHz. The loop locks only when the input frequency falls inside the capture range; once locked, it tracks over the wider lock range.
chapters.trap: Swapping capture range and lock range, and expecting the loop to lock on an input far outside both.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.6, since the 555 makes a simple VCO. Unit 4: oscillator feedback and free-running frequency.
chapters.leave: Frequency synthesiser design with programmable dividers to later courses. Detailed loop-filter stability analysis to a control-systems course.

chapters.idea: A DAC adds binary-weighted currents into one node, and the R-2R ladder does it with only two resistor values so the network can be built accurately on an IC.
chapters.depth: Weighted-resistor DAC: binary-weighted input resistors R, 2R, 4R … 2^(n−1)R with a summing op-amp, giving V_out = −V_ref(R_f/R)(b_{n−1}/2^(n−1) + … + b_0/1); requires a resistor spread of 2^(n−1) to 1 and is impractical beyond about 4 bits. R-2R ladder DAC: only R and 2R, V_out = −V_ref × D/2^n, where D is the decimal value of the n-bit input word. Terms: resolution, LSB = V_ref/2^n, full-scale output, settling time, monotonicity, glitch, offset and gain error. Bipolar (offset) output and multiplying DACs in some syllabi. Depth: compute the output for a given word, the LSB size, and the maximum output.

figure.title: Bit weights in a 4-bit weighted-resistor DAC
figure.aria: Four rows, one per bit, giving the input resistor and the fraction of the reference current that each bit contributes; the top bit needs the largest resistor.

chapters.example: An 8-bit R-2R DAC has V_ref = 5 V and R_f = R. The input word is 10110010. D = 128 + 32 + 16 + 2 = 178. V_out = −5 × 178/256 = −3.48 V. The LSB is 5/256 = 19.5 mV. The largest output is 5 × 255/256 = 4.98 V, one LSB below V_ref.
chapters.trap: Assuming the maximum output equals V_ref. Full scale is (2ⁿ − 1)/2ⁿ × V_ref, and the sign is inverted because the ladder feeds the op-amp's virtual ground.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6: inverting summing amplifier and virtual ground. Unit 5: op-amp offset and settling.
chapters.leave: Multiplying DACs, INL and DNL measurement, and self-calibration to later courses.
chapters.added: Included because almost every ADC in Chapter 7.9 contains a DAC.

chapters.idea: Four architectures trade speed against resolution and accuracy: flash compares all at once, successive approximation searches bit by bit, dual-slope measures a time ratio, and sigma-delta oversamples and shapes noise.
chapters.depth: Flash (simultaneous) ADC: a resistor string and 2ⁿ − 1 comparators, conversion in one clock, fastest, low resolution, high input capacitance. Successive approximation: comparator plus internal DAC, one bit per clock, n clocks per conversion, binary search, the workhorse of 8 to 16 bits. Dual-slope: run-up for a fixed T1 = 2ⁿ T_clk integrating V_in, then de-integrate against V_ref; the count when the integrator returns to zero is the code, T2 = T1 V_in/V_ref; immune to clock-frequency and capacitor drift, slow, ideal for panel meters. Sigma-delta, taught at only a few universities: oversampling, noise shaping, a 1-bit comparator, a digital decimation filter. Terms: sampling rate, quantisation error, conversion time, aperture time, resolution versus accuracy. Depth: pick the right part for a stated speed and resolution and compute the code or the timing.

figure.title: ADC families compared
figure.aria: Four rows, one per ADC family, listing the number of comparators, the relative speed and the typical resolution; flash is the only one with many comparators.

chapters.example: A 10-bit dual-slope ADC has V_ref = 2 V and a 100 kHz clock, so T_clk = 10 µs. Run-up time T1 = 2¹⁰ × 10 µs = 10.24 ms. With V_in = 1.5 V the de-integration time is T2 = T1 × V_in/V_ref = 10.24 ms × 0.75 = 7.68 ms. The counter reads 7.68 ms / 10 µs = 768 out of 1024, so the code is 768.
chapters.trap: Counting 2ⁿ comparators in a flash ADC instead of 2ⁿ − 1, and calling an SAR ADC slow because it takes n clocks — it is fast, just not as fast as flash.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.8 for the DAC inside the SAR and dual-slope converters. Unit 6: comparator and sample-and-hold.
chapters.leave: Quantisation-noise derivations, decimation filter design and ADC testing to advanced courses.
